State of Karnataka]. Therefore, the bench of Justice HP Sandesh and Justice B Pramod dismissed an appeal challenging the acquittal of two accused in a case concerning the death of a child. “Merely because the accused refused to give back his ball and directed him to bring his father cannot be taken as an abetment to commit suicide," the Court said. The Court held that the prosecution failed to establish the essential ingredients of abetment under Section 107 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), which was necessary to sustain a charge of abetment of suicide of child under Section 305 IPC. Justice H P Sandesh, Justice B Pramod The case related to the death of a child, Kiran, on February 1, 2019. According to the prosecution, the child was playing volleyball outside his house when the ball accidentally entered the accused's shop and broke a glass pane. When the child went to retrieve the ball, the accused allegedly refused to return it and scolded him. They told him to bring his father and warned that they would teach him a lesson. The prosecution alleged that the incident caused the child mental distress and he went home and died by suicide. The accused were booked for abetment of suicide under Section 305 IPC. The trial court acquitted the accused on January 7, 2025. The complainant then approached the High Court, seeking reversal of the acquittal and conviction of the accused under Section 305 read with Section 34 IPC. The High Court found that the prosecution had failed to establish any positive act by the accused which drove the child to commit suicide. The Bench noted that there was neither any positive action in close proximity to the suicide nor evidence of continuous physical or mental torture by the accused. “The ingredients of mens rea cannot be assumed to be present; they have to be vital and conspicuous," the bench further held. The Court also noted that there were no eyewitnesses to the alleged conversation between the child and the accused. The father and mother were found to be hearsay witnesses. items.title: Corruption in TVK government? | CM Vijay | Shabbir Ahmed | TNM Tamil
items.summary: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay has promised a corruption-free governance as a central promise of his administration. In his first months in office, he has spoken about strengthening vigilance mechanisms, ensuring transparency in government contracts and taking action against officials involved in corruption. But how much of this is translating into change on the ground? Tamil Nadu already has institutions such as the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) to investigate and act on corruption complaints. Yet questions over the independence of these mechanisms, delays in investigations and the role of political and administrative approvals remain. In this week’s episode of Yen Endra Kelvi, Shabbir Ahmed speaks to Jayaram Venkatesh, Convener of Arappor Iyakkam, to examine whether government anti-corruption steps becoming more effective, how officials are responding to the new government’s approach, and discuss about building a system that can sustain the fight against corruption.

items.title: Chennai: 285 with criminal records detained in crime prevention drive
items.summary: Nearly 285 people with criminal records, including history-sheeters, were arrested in a special drive conducted across Chennai, with police claiming that the operation was aimed at preventing crime and curbing the activities of habitual offenders. They were detained during an intensive search operation carried out from Thursday, September 10 night to Friday, September 11 evening, following directions from Greater Chennai Police Commissioner A Amalraj. The operation was conducted under the supervision of Deputy Commissioners and led by Assistant Commissioners, Inspectors and other police personnel. Of the 285 people detained, 108 were from the North Zone, 38 from the West Zone, 94 from the South Zone and 45 from the East Zone. “During the operation, the teams detained 285 individuals with criminal backgrounds, whose history sheets are maintained at various police stations in the city. They are being questioned to ascertain their current activities and possible involvement in recent offences,” a senior police officer said. However, the police's classification of people as having “criminal backgrounds” or being history-sheeters does not, by itself, establish that they have committed a recent offence. History sheets are police records maintained on people considered to have criminal antecedents, and the use of such records for preventive policing has previously raised concerns over surveillance, arbitrary detention and the targeting of people without a specific allegation against them. Police Commissioner Amalraj said such special drives would continue and that stringent legal action would be taken against those involved in criminal activities. He also instructed Additional Commissioners and other senior officers to closely monitor the movements of people with criminal antecedents, dangerous offenders and those released from prison on bail. Amalraj further directed officers to strengthen patrolling and vehicle checks and take stringent action against drunk driving.
